summary: Specifies how to use DNS SRV records to find services for the AFS distributed file system, and how to read priority and weight values. It deprecates the AFSDB record from RFC 1183 for locating AFS database servers. It is a proposed standard.

subtitle: How AFS clients find a cell's database servers with DNS SRV records instead of the old AFSDB record.

tldr.problem: AFS clients needed to find the VLDB and PTS servers of a cell, but the AFSDB record from RFC 1183 has no priority, no port and no protocol, and assumes both services run on one host.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines SRV labels for the two services, _afs3-vlserver and _afs3-prserver, and says how the SRV priority and weight values map onto the preference ranks AFS clients already use.
tldr.outcome: AFSDB is deprecated for locating AFS cell database servers, though cells are still advised to publish AFSDB records for older clients. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and was later updated by RFC 8553.

facts.label: Protocol for the current AFS
facts.value: udp, that is Rx over UDP

today: RFC 5864 is a Proposed Standard published in April 2010. It updated RFC 1183 by deprecating AFSDB for locating AFS cell database servers, and it was later updated by RFC 8553.

sections.title: Overview and Rationale
sections.content:
AFS is a distributed file system. Its most widely used implementations are OpenAFS and ARLA. AFS is organized administratively into cells. Each AFS cell consists of one or more Volume Location Database (VLDB) servers, one or more Protection Service (PTS) servers, and one or more file servers and volume servers, plus possible additional services not relevant to this document. Data stored in AFS is divided into collections of files called volumes.

An AFS protocol client, when accessing a file within a specific AFS cell, first contacts a VLDB server for that cell to determine the file server for the AFS volume in which that file is located, and then contacts that file server directly to access the file. A client may also need to contact a PTS server for that cell to register before accessing files in that cell, or to query protection database information.

An AFS client therefore needs to determine, for a given AFS cell, the VLDB and possibly the PTS servers for that cell. Traditionally the VLDB and PTS servers are provided by the same host. Once the client is in contact with the VLDB server, it locates file and volume servers through AFS protocol queries to the VLDB server. Originally, VLDB server information was configured separately on each client in a file called the CellServDB file, and RFC 1183 specified the DNS resource record AFSDB to locate VLDB servers for AFS.

Subsequent to RFC 1183, a general DNS resource record was defined by RFC 2782 for service location for any service. The DNS SRV record has several advantages over the AFSDB record. AFSDB records do not support priority or ranking, leaving AFS cell administrators without a way to indicate which VLDB servers clients should prefer. They do not include protocol or port information, implicitly assuming that all VLDB servers will be contacted over the standard port and the UDP, and future changes to the AFS protocol may require separate VLDB server lists for UDP and TCP traffic. Clients using AFSDB records must assume that VLDB and PTS services are provided by the same host, but it may be useful to separate VLDB servers from PTS servers. And DNS SRV records are in widespread use, whereas AFSDB records are a little-known and little-supported corner of the DNS protocol. For those reasons, it is desirable to move AFS service location from the AFSDB record to DNS SRV records.
sections.plainLanguage: AFS is a distributed file system split into administrative areas called cells. A client that wants a file first asks a cell's directory server which host holds that file, then talks to that host directly. The old way to find those directory servers was the AFSDB DNS record, which is too limited: it cannot say which server to prefer, it cannot say a port, and it assumes two services live on the same machine. The SRV record, already widely used, can say all of that.

sections.title: Scope
sections.content:
This document describes the format and use of DNS SRV records for AFS service location and deprecates the AFSDB record. It also provides guidance for transition from the AFSDB record to DNS SRV records and recommendations for backward compatibility.

Documentation of the AFS protocol, the exact purpose and use of the VLDB and PTS services, and other information about AFS are outside the scope of this document. AFSDB records may also be used for locating servers for the Open Software Foundation's Distributed Computing Environment authenticated naming system, as described in RFC 1183. Service location for DCE servers is outside the scope of this document and is not modified by this specification.
sections.plainLanguage: The document is about the DNS records only. It does not describe the AFS protocol itself, and it does not change how DCE naming servers are found.

sections.title: DNS SRV RRs for AFS
sections.content:
The label of a DNS SRV record is _<service>._<proto>.<name>. Two values of the service part advertise servers providing AFS services: afs3-vlserver for servers providing AFS VLDB services, and afs3-prserver for servers providing AFS PTS services. Other AFS services, such as file and volume management services, are located through the VLDB service and therefore do not use DNS SRV records.

The protocol part MUST be udp for the current AFS protocol, which uses Rx over UDP. Other values may be used for future revisions of the AFS protocol supporting other protocols, such as Rx over TCP. The name part MUST be the AFS cell name for which the identified server provides AFS services. Clients MUST query DNS SRV records only for a name value exactly matching the AFS cell of interest, and MUST NOT remove leading components to search for more general records. The AFS cell prod.example.com and the AFS cell example.com are entirely different cells in the AFS protocol, and VLDB servers for the latter cannot provide information for the former.

Because of this, DNS SRV records can only be used to locate AFS services for cells whose naming matches the structure of the DNS. This is not a requirement of the AFS protocol, but sites creating new AFS cells SHOULD use names that follow the structure of the DNS and that result in DNS SRV records under their administrative control. That both permits the use of DNS SRV records instead of client configuration and helps avoid naming conflicts between separate AFS cells.

DNS SRV records include a priority and a weight. Clients MUST attempt to contact the target host with the lowest-numbered priority they can reach. AFS clients that use a ranked algorithm MUST therefore assign a sufficiently distinct rank to targets with different priorities, so that targets with a higher-numbered priority are only contacted if all targets with a lower-numbered priority are inaccessible. If there are multiple targets with an equal priority, the weight value SHOULD be used as input to a weighted algorithm for selecting servers, with larger weights given a proportionately higher probability of being selected. In the presence of records containing weights greater than 0, records with weight 0 should have a very small chance of being selected. A weight of 0 SHOULD be used if all targets with that priority are weighted equally. AFS clients MAY take network performance and other protocol metrics into account along with the SRV weights, but such information MUST NOT override the priority information in the record.

DNS SRV records, like all DNS records, have a time-to-live, after which the record information is no longer valid. Records SHOULD be discarded after their TTL and after the DNS query repeated, and any information derived from them, such as preference ranks, MUST be discarded when the record is expired. Implementations are not required to re-run the weighted server selection algorithm for each call, and MAY reuse the results until the records expire, which may affect the load distribution the records provide, so server operators should account for that when setting the TTL. AFS clients MAY remember which targets are inaccessible by that client and ignore them when determining which server to contact first, but SHOULD have a mechanism to retry those targets and reconsider them according to their current priority and weight if they become accessible again.
sections.plainLanguage: Two record names are used: one for the servers that hold the cell's directory, and one for the servers that handle authentication. The protocol part is udp, because that is what the current AFS protocol uses. The cell name must match exactly: prod.example.com and example.com are different cells, and the servers of one cannot answer for the other. The priority says which servers to try first, and the weight spreads the load among servers with the same priority.

sections.title: Interpretation as AFS Preference Ranks
sections.content:
Several AFS implementations use a ranking algorithm that assigns numbers representing a preference rank to each server when the client first contacts that AFS cell, and then prefers the server with the lowest rank unless that server goes down. Clients using this algorithm SHOULD assign their ranks as follows.

First, sort the targets by priority and assign a base rank value to each target based on its priority. Each base rank value MUST be sufficiently different from the base rank assigned to any higher-numbered priority, so that higher-numbered targets will only be attempted if lower-numbered targets cannot be reached. The numeric value of a priority has no meaning: only the ordering of distinct priority values between multiple SRV record targets needs to be reflected in the base ranks.

Second, for each group of targets with the same priority, follow the algorithm in RFC 2782 to order those targets, then assign those targets ranks formed by incrementing the base weight for that priority, so that the first selected target has the lowest rank, the second the next-lowest, and so on.

After the ranks have been assigned, the AFS client MAY adjust them dynamically based on network performance and other protocol metrics, provided that such adjustments are sufficiently small compared to the difference between base ranks that they cannot cause servers with a higher-numbered priority to be contacted instead of a server with a lower-numbered priority. The TTL of the DNS SRV records MUST be honoured by invalidating and regenerating the server preference ranks with new DNS information once the TTL has expired, although accumulated network and protocol metrics may be retained and reapplied to the new rankings.

AFS server preference ranks are conventionally numbers between 1 and 65535, while DNS SRV record priorities are numbers between 0 and 65535. An implementation following this algorithm could therefore encounter problems assigning sufficiently distinct base rank values in the exceptional case of very large numbers of SRV record targets with meaningfully distinct priorities, but a cell configuration with thousands of SRV targets with distinct priorities is highly improbable. A client encountering a record with more distinct priority values than can be correctly represented as base ranks SHOULD fall back to generating ranks based solely on priorities, ignoring other rank inputs, and disabling dynamic adjustment of ranks. Implementations MUST be able to assign distinct base ranks as described above for at least ten distinct priority values.
sections.plainLanguage: Many AFS clients already rank servers and use the lowest rank first. This section says how to build those ranks from the DNS records. Give each priority its own band of ranks, with enough space between bands that the client will only move to a lower-priority server when it has to. Inside a band, use the SRV weighting to order the servers. Measured performance may nudge the ranks a little, but never across a band boundary, and the ranks are rebuilt when the DNS records expire.

sections.title: Use of AFSDB RRs
sections.content:
Since many AFS client implementations currently support AFSDB records but do not support DNS SRV records, AFS cells providing DNS SRV records SHOULD also provide AFSDB records. Be aware that AFSDB records do not provide priority or weighting information, so all servers listed in them are treated as equal, and they do not provide port information.

An AFS cell using DNS SRV records SHOULD therefore also provide an AFSDB record listing all AFS servers for which the following statements are all true: the server provides both VLDB and PTS service on the standard ports, 7003 and 7002 respectively; the server provides these services via Rx over UDP; and the server either has the lowest-numbered priority of those listed in the DNS SRV records, or the AFS cell administrator believes it reasonable for clients using AFSDB records to use this server by preference.

This is a default recommendation. Cell administrators MAY use different lists of servers in the AFSDB records and the DNS SRV records, for specific effects based on local knowledge of which clients use which record type. AFS servers SHOULD NOT be advertised with AFSDB records unless they provide VLDB and PTS services via UDP on the standard ports. The RFC stops short of a prohibition, because it may be useful in some unusual circumstances to advertise, via an AFSDB record, a server that provides only one of the two services, but a reader should be aware that such a configuration may confuse legacy clients. An AFS cell SHOULD have at least one VLDB and at least one PTS server providing service on the standard ports of 7003 and 7002, since clients without DNS SRV record support cannot locate servers on non-standard ports.

Clients SHOULD query DNS SRV records by default, and SHOULD then fall back on AFSDB records if no DNS SRV records are found. In the absence of DNS SRV records, an AFSDB record of subtype 1 SHOULD be treated as equivalent to the pair of DNS SRV records _afs3-vlserver._udp.<cell> <ttl> IN SRV 0 0 7003 <hostname> and _afs3-prserver._udp.<cell> <ttl> IN SRV 0 0 7002 <hostname>, where the cell is the label of the AFSDB record, the TTL is its TTL, and the hostname is the hostname value of the AFSDB record, which is the fully-qualified domain name of the server.
sections.plainLanguage: Old clients only understand the AFSDB record, so a cell that publishes SRV records should keep an AFSDB record too, listing only the servers that run both services over UDP on the standard ports. Clients should try SRV first and fall back to AFSDB. An AFSDB record is then read as two SRV records with priority and weight of zero, on ports 7003 and 7002.

sections.title: Example
sections.content:
The example zone file shows a range of possibilities: TCP AFS services, separation of a PTS server from a VLDB server, and the use of non-standard ports. These are features that either assume future AFS protocol development or are not widely supported by current clients, so the example is intended to show the range of what AFS DNS SRV records can express rather than to be a practical example for an existing cell. In this example the AFS cell name is example.com.

afsdb1, afsdb2 and afsdb3 all provide VLDB service via UDP. The first two have the same priority but have weights indicating that afsdb1 should get about twice as many clients as afsdb2. afsdb3 should only be used for UDP VLDB service if afsdb1 and afsdb2 are not accessible, and it provides that service on a non-standard port, 65500. Only one host, afsdb1, provides UDP PTS service. afsdb3 provides a hypothetical TCP version of AFS VLDB and PTS service on the standard ports, and is the only server providing these services over TCP for this cell. Such a TCP-based AFS protocol did not exist at the time the document was written. An AFSDB record is provided for backward compatibility with older clients, and it lists only afsdb1, since only that host provides both VLDB and PTS service over UDP on the standard ports.
sections.plainLanguage: The worked example puts three servers in one cell with different priorities and weights, separates the authentication server from the directory servers, and shows a non-standard port. The old AFSDB record is kept for older clients and lists only the one server that runs both services on the standard ports.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Use of DNS SRV records for AFS service locations poses the same security issues as the existing AFSDB records. Unless the integrity and authenticity of the DNS response are checked, an attacker may forge DNS replies and thereby direct clients at a VLDB or PTS server under the control of the attacker. From there the attacker may deceive an AFS client about the volumes and file servers in a cell and about the contents of files and directories in that cell. If the client uses cell data in a trusted way, such as by executing programs out of that AFS cell or using data from the cell as input to other programs, the attacker may be able to further compromise the security of the client and trick it into taking action under the attacker's control.

This attack can be prevented if the server is authenticated, since the client can then detect a failure to authenticate the attacker's servers and thereby detect possible impersonation. However, this applies only to authenticated AFS access, and much AFS access is unauthenticated. Furthermore, clients after a failure to authenticate may fall back to unauthenticated access, which the attacker's servers may permit.

Using an integrity-protected DNS system such as DNSSEC can prevent this attack via DNS. However, the underlying vulnerability is inherent in the current AFS protocol and may be exploited in ways other than DNS forgery, such as by forging the results of VLDB queries for an AFS cell. Addressing it properly requires changes to the AFS protocol allowing clients to always authenticate AFS services and discard unauthenticated data. Even in the absence of a DNS system with integrity protection, the addition of DNS SRV records does not make this vulnerability more severe, only opens another equivalent point of attack.
sections.plainLanguage: Finding a server through DNS means trusting the DNS answer. If an attacker can forge it, the client is sent to a server the attacker controls, which can then lie about the contents of the cell's files. DNSSEC closes that door, but the same trick can still be played inside the AFS protocol itself, and much AFS access is not authenticated at all. The RFC is clear that fixing this properly needs changes to AFS itself.

viz.caption: HOW TO TURN THE RECORDS INTO PREFERENCE RANKS

items.title: Sort by priority
items.text: Give each priority its own band of ranks, far enough apart that a higher priority is only tried when the lower ones fail.

items.title: Order within a priority
items.text: Use the SRV weighted algorithm, then step the ranks up one at a time.

items.title: Adjust with measurements
items.text: Network performance may nudge the ranks, but never across a priority boundary.

items.title: Expire with the TTL
items.text: Regenerate the ranks when the SRV records expire; the measurements may be kept.

data.title: AFS services for the cell example.com
data.code:
$ORIGIN example.com.
@                    SOA   dns.example.com. root.example.com. (
                             2009100201 3600 3600 604800 86400 )
                    NS    dns.example.com.
_afs3-vlserver._udp  SRV   0 2 7003 afsdb1.example.com.
_afs3-vlserver._udp  SRV   0 4 7003 afsdb2.example.com.
_afs3-vlserver._udp  SRV   1 0 65500 afsdb3.example.com.

_afs3-vlserver._tcp  SRV   0 0 7003 afsdb3.example.com.

_afs3-prserver._udp  SRV   0 0 7002 afsdb1.example.com.

_afs3-prserver._tcp  SRV   0 0 7002 afsdb3.example.com.

@                    AFSDB 1 afsdb1.example.com.
